Date of judgment/order 17.07.2026 Date of Institution : 21.09.2020 Date of Reserving Judgment/Order : 06.06.2026 Date of Pronouncement of Judgment/Order : 17.07.2026 ARGUING COUNSELS: CT Case No. 4268/2020 The Riddhi Siddhi Cooperative Urban Thrift & Credit Society Ltd. Vs. Mohd. Aashiq Mirza Page 2 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.17 16:25:15 +0530 Ld. Counsel for the complainant : Sh. Abhishek Rai Ld. Counsel for the Accused : Sh. Mohd. Zubair Saifi JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this Court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by the complainant The Riddhi Siddhi Cooperative Urban Thrift and Credit Society Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "complainant") against Mohd. Aashiq Mirza (hereinafter referred to as the "accused") under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 read with Section 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). Brief facts of the case: 2. It is the case of the complainant, A. That, the accused is one of the member of the complainant society and had applied personal loan of Rs. 2,00,000/- before the complainant society through loan application. That, the complainant society sanctioned the personal loan of Rs. 2,00,000/- to the accused on 02.04.2016 at 16.20% per annum and the accused acknowledged the loan through a payment voucher dated 02.04.2016. That, the accused in discharge of his liability issued a cheque bearing no. 000011 dated 27.02.2020 in the sum of Rs. 2,08,977/- drawn on Bank of India, Sangam Vihar Branch, New Delhi in favour of the complainant. That, on the assurance of the accused, the complainant presented the cheque in question in his bank however the same was returned unpaid with remark "Funds Insufficient" vide return memo dated 29.02.2020. CT Case No. 4268/2020 The Riddhi Siddhi Cooperative Urban Thrift & Credit Society Ltd. Vs. Mohd. Aashiq Mirza Page 3 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.17 16:25:20 +0530 B. In these circumstances, the complainant got issued a statutory legal demand notice to the accused person through his counsel, dated 13.03.2020, thereby requiring the accused person to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheques within a period of 15 days from the receipt of the said notice. The said notice under Sec. 138 of NI Act was sent to the accused person through Registered AD/Speed Post/Courier at their correct address. That despite service of the above stated notice of demand, the Accused person has deliberately and willfully failed to comply with the said notice of demand and has failed to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within the stipulated period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. Consequently, this case was filed by the complainant against the accused persons, which was within the limitation period as laid down u/s 138 , NI Act. 3. In the pre-summoning evidence, the complainant examined himself on affidavit being Ex. CW1/1 and relied on documents Ex. CW1/A to Ex. CW1/K. 4. Upon prima facie consideration of the pre-summoning evidence, the accused person was summoned. 5. Upon the appearance of the accused, notice under Section 251 CrPC was served upon him on 13.10.2023 to which he pleaded not guilty. The accused has admitted his signatures on the cheque in question, however has denied receiving the legal demand notice. The accused has further stated that he had taken a loan of Rs. 2 lakhs from the complainant company which was payable within 3 years by way of EMI's, against which Rs. 32,000/- was deposited with the complainant as security and the accused had paid 8-9 EMIs of Rs. 8000/- each. The accused has CT Case No. 4268/2020 The Riddhi Siddhi Cooperative Urban Thrift & Credit Society Ltd. Vs. Mohd. Aashiq Mirza Page 4 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.17 16:25:30 +0530 admitted to issuance of cheque as a security cheque against the loan in question and outstanding liability of Rs. 1 lakh towards the complainant. 6. Vide separate statement of accused, admissions and denial u/s 294 CrPC was done and witness no. 2 and 3 were dropped from the list of complainant witnesses. 7. CW-1 was examined-in-chief, cross-examined and discharged. Thereby, CE was closed on 08.10.2024. Accordingly, matter proceeded to the stage of recording the statement of the accused person. 8. Statement of accused under Section 313 CrPC read with Section 281 CrPC was recorded wherein the accused opted to lead defence evidence. DW-1 was examined in chief, cross-examined and discharged. Thereafter, DE was closed vide order of this court on 16.05.2026. 9. Thereafter, the matter was listed for final arguments. After hearing the final arguments from both sides, the matter was reserved for pronouncement of judgment. 10. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: I. drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; CT Case No. 4268/2020 The Riddhi Siddhi Cooperative Urban Thrift & Credit Society Ltd. Vs. Mohd. Aashiq Mirza Page 5 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.07.17 16:25:46 +0530 III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. RBI in its notification DBOD.AML BC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. The offence under Section 138 , NI Act is made out against the drawer of the cheque, only when all the aforementioned ingredients are fulfilled. 11. Analysing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa [AIR 2019 SC 1983] held that: Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates that a presumption be drawn that the cheque in question was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. CT Case No. 4268/2020 The Riddhi Siddhi Cooperative Urban Thrift & Credit Society Ltd. Vs. Mohd. Aashiq Mirza Page 6 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.17 16:26:03 +0530 II. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. III. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. IV. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. It is therefore implied that the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the presumptions under Section 118(a) and Section 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. Appreciation of evidence and marshalling of facts: 12. Issuance of cheque: The complainant has filed on record the original cheque, i.e., bearing no. 000011 dated 27.02.2020 for Rs. 2,08,977/- drawn on Bank of India, Sangam Vihar Branch, New Delhi (Ex. CW1/D). In notice under Section 251 CrPC, the accused has admitted that the cheque in dispute belongs to him. It is also not disputed that the cheque in question is not drawn on the account CT Case No. 4268/2020 The Riddhi Siddhi Cooperative Urban Thrift & Credit Society Ltd. Vs. Mohd. Aashiq Mirza Page 7 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.17 16:26:11 +0530 maintained by the accused and it is impliedly admitted therefore that the accused is the drawer of the cheque. Therefore, ingredient number I stands fulfilled in the present case. 13. Presentment and dishonor of cheque: As per the RBI guidelines, it is essential for the cheque in question be to presented within a period of three months from the date on which they are drawn and the same be returned as unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque. In the case at hand, the cheque in question was returned vide return memo dated 29.02.2020 (Ex. CW1/E) due to the reason "Funds Insufficient." By implication thereof, the cheque was presented within three months and the same was returned. Therefore, Ingredient number III & IV stand fulfilled in the present case. 14. Legal demand notice and payment by the accused thereof: The legal notice dated 13.03.2020 (Ex. CW1/F) was dispatched on 13.03.2020 vide Speed Post (Ex. CW1/G), i.e., within 30 days of return of the bank memo indicating cheques in question being unpaid. The fact that the legal demand notice has made a clear and unambiguous demand for payment of the cheque in question is not disputed. The accused has not admitted to the receiving of legal demand notice in notice u/s 251 CrPC. However, as per the presumption raised under Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and Section 27 of General Clauses Act, if the legal demand notice is sent at the correct address, then the same shall be deemed to have been duly served, as per the precedent laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 3 SCC (Cri). The ingredient number V is fulfilled by virtue of giving of legal demand notice within 30 days from the bank CT Case No. 4268/2020 The Riddhi Siddhi Cooperative Urban Thrift & Credit Society Ltd. Vs. Mohd. Aashiq Mirza Page 8 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.17 16:26:18 +0530 return memo. The receipt of legal demand notice by the accused is deemed to be admitted as per the discussion above. 15. Moving on, it is not disputed that the accused has not made the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal demand notice. Therefore, ingredient number VI also stands fulfilled in the present case. Presumption under Section 118A read with Section 139 , NI Act 16. The NI Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque, i.e., complainant; firstly, with regard to the issuance of cheque for consideration, as contained in Section 118(a) and secondly, with regard to the fact that the holder of cheque received the same for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, as contained in Section 139 of the Act. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its judgment titled Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 held that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. Once a probable defence is raised, then the onus is shifted CT Case No. 4268/2020 The Riddhi Siddhi Cooperative Urban Thrift & Credit Society Ltd. Vs. Mohd. Aashiq Mirza Page 9 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.17 16:26:24 +0530 to the complainant to establish that a legally enforceable liability existed in his favour and the burden of proof on the complainant in this case is that of "beyond reasonable doubt." 17. The accused can rebut the presumption as raised under Section 138 , NI Act by: (a) putting forth his defence at the time of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC; (b) cross-examining the complainant; (c) when statement of accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC; (d) or by leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. Rebuttal of Presumption by Accused as to existence of legally enforceable debt 18. In light of the above discussion, since the accused has admitted to issuance of cheques, admitted the signatures on the cheques and legal notice has also been deemed to be served, what is left to be seen is whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption against him, i.e., whether the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt? 19. In the present case, in order to discharge his initial burden to prove the abovementioned ingredients, the complainant relied upon the affidavit of the complainant being Ex. CW1/1 and placed on record documents mentioned CT Case No. 4268/2020 The Riddhi Siddhi Cooperative Urban Thrift & Credit Society Ltd. Vs. Mohd. Aashiq Mirza Page 10 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.07.17 16:26:29 +0530 hereinbefore. The case of the complainant is that the accused had taken a loan from the complainant on interest and had issued the cheque in question towards discharge of his liability. Per Contra, the defence of the accused is that they had repaid certain amount towards the liability and they do not owe liability as mentioned on the cheque in question. 20. The primary defence of the accused is that the loan in the sum of Rs. 2,00,000/- was availed by the accused and out of the same, he has paid 8-9 installments of Rs. 8000/- each alongwith some payment by way of cash and therefore the liability of the accused is not what is mentioned in the cheque in question and the present case is hit by the principle laid down by the Apex Court in Dasrathbhai Trikambhai Patel v. Hitesh Mahendrabhai . Ld. Counsel for the accused has also placed on record receipts for indicating repayment Ex. CW1/D1 to Ex. CW1/D4. 21. A bare perusal of the loan agreement Ex. CW1/A indicates that the accused had voluntarily signed the agreement which mentioned the deposit for share money and other deductions and interest at a rate of 16.20% p.a. The accused has nowhere denied his signatures on the loan agreement. Furthermore, the accused in his DW-1 has admitted that he has signed the loan application form and loan bond and has admitted the interest rate on the loan agreement. Therefore, the loan agreement and its contents stand proved. A bare perusal of the amount mentioned on the receipt Ex. CW1/D1 & Ex. CW1/D2 are security deposit amount which is a fee advanced at the time of availing loan and includes share money and other deposits which are to be paid as per the agreement on record Ex. CW1/A. After deducting the amount of share money and deposits, the amount repaid by the accused is adjusted against CT Case No. 4268/2020 The Riddhi Siddhi Cooperative Urban Thrift & Credit Society Ltd. Vs. Mohd. Aashiq Mirza Page 11 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.07.17 16:26:35 +0530 the liability towards the loan in question. A bare perusal of the statement of account Ex. CW1/C (Colly.) indicate the repayment by the accused on 13.08.2017 and on 20.07.2018 excluding the share money/ compulsory deposit/ recurring deposit as agreed to in the agreement by accused Ex. CW1/A, therefore, the argument of the accused that entire repayment by accused as mentioned in Ex. DW1 to DW4 is not reflected in statement of accounts of complainant, does not stand. The accused has further argued that the complainant has failed to mention about all other repayments made by the accused to the complainant partly online and partly in cash. However, the accused has neither brought any acknowledgement receipt nor any other document indicating the repayment of the loan by the accused and lesser liability of the accused than what is mentioned in the cheque in question on the date of the presentation of the cheque, i.e., 27.02.2020. Therefore, the argument of the accused that the present complaint is hit by the principle laid down in Dasrathbhai (supra) is not substantiated. 22. In the present case, the accused has failed to even create any doubt, let alone discharging his burden of proof to rebut the presumption u/s 139 , NI Act. Further, the accused is obligated to set up a probable defence and not a possible defence, i.e., there should be some credible material or circumstance on record to show that the defence taken by the accused is a probable one. In the present case, firstly, the accused has not brought any witness on record nor brought any documentary evidence on record to substantiate his claims. It is the duty of the accused to punch holes in the story of the complainant which he has not been able to do. Secondly, the complainant has brought documentary evidence so as to prove his version of the story alongwith the benefit of presumption raised u/s 139 , NI Act in his favour. CT Case No. 4268/2020 The Riddhi Siddhi Cooperative Urban Thrift & Credit Society Ltd. Vs. Mohd. Aashiq Mirza Page 12 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.07.17 16:26:43 +0530 23. In light of the discussion above, this Court is of the view that the accused has not been able to rebut the presumption against him and therefore ingredient no. II has been fulfilled in the present case. Conclusion: 24. In view of the evidence adduced, documents put forth and arguments advanced by the parties and further in view of the above discussion, the court is of the considered view that accused Mohd. Aashiq Mirza is guilty of offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and accordingly, accused is hereby convicted under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 25. Copy of this judgment be given to the convict free of cost as per rules. PRONOUNCED IN THE OPEN COURT TODAY ON 17th July, 2026.
